items.title: The Information: SoftBank's Son explored a roughly $1 trillion buyout of SK hynix; idea since dropped
items.summary: SoftBank Group CEO Masayoshi Son sounded out Wall Street institutions about financing a takeover of SK hynix at roughly $1 trillion, according to The Information, as relayed by Reuters. The price reportedly reflected SK hynix's recent peak value plus a 40% control premium. SK hynix's market value is now about $578B. SoftBank said it reviews many opportunities and this one is no longer under active consideration. SK hynix said it had no knowledge of the matter and noted that any foreign acquisition would need prior Korean government approval.
items.why_it_matters: It shows how far Son has been willing to go to control AI memory supply, though Korean approval rules and the size make a deal impractical. The report lands as memory stocks swing sharply in the AI selloff.

items.title: Thinking Machines releases Inkling 2 Mini, a 26.4B open-weight looped MoE that runs on a laptop
items.summary: Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini under Apache 2.0, a mixture-of-experts model with 26.4B total and 3.4B active parameters that needs roughly 20GB of memory and has a 1M-token context window. It is a looped transformer: its middle layers run multiple times per token (three, per one report), so it does more internal reasoning per token. Weights are on Hugging Face, it is on Tinker for inference and fine-tuning, and Ollama supports it on Macs with at least 32GB of RAM. The lab claims it leads open-weight models under 100B parameters on DeepSWE v1.1 (48.2%) and Vals Index v2.2 (46.5%).
items.why_it_matters: A credible US lab shipping a laptop-class open-weight agentic coder, with a looped architecture, adds competition to Chinese small open models and to cloud-only coding agents. It is also Thinking Machines' clearest bid for developer mindshare beyond Tinker.

items.title: Alpöge and Buckmaster post AI-assisted claim of unforced finite-time blowup for 3D Navier-Stokes
items.summary: NYU's Tristan Buckmaster and Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge posted a 79-page paper dated Nov 20 claiming finite-time blowup for the 3D Navier-Stokes equations with no external force, the version most mathematicians consider the 'real' problem. OpenAI's September result needed a precisely tuned forcing term. Buckmaster said the write-up is unpolished and heavily LLM-assisted, using Anthropic and OpenAI models including Codex. A companion Euler paper with Matei Coiculescu comes with a Lean formalisation. Terence Tao called the paper technically human-readable with a broadly clear strategy, but said more work is needed before it is a properly written proof.
items.why_it_matters: If it holds, it would be a much stronger AI-assisted result than OpenAI's forced-blowup proof, and it sharpens the credit dispute between Buckmaster and OpenAI. It lands a day after Alpöge's Riemann-hypothesis claim, so AI-assisted proofs of famous problems are arriving faster than experts can check them.

items.title: Signal blocks screenshots by default on iOS and Android to keep OS-level AI agents out of chats
items.summary: Signal now blocks screenshots by default on iOS 27 and adds a 'Block Siri AI' toggle, on by default, which also hides chats in the App Switcher. On supported Android devices, its Screen Security feature switches on when an AI assistant tries to read the screen. President Meredith Whittaker called OS-built AI agents an 'existential threat' to Signal. Signal concedes the gaps: the block won't work on every Android device, there is no reliable block on macOS, agents may still reach data through the filesystem, and a contact who disables protections exposes the conversation on their own device.
items.why_it_matters: It is the first major app to turn on anti-agent defences by default on phones, which puts pressure on Apple and Google to give apps enforceable opt-outs from on-device agents such as Siri AI, Gemini and Meta's Muse. Agent builders that rely on screen-reading should expect more apps to follow.

items.title: OpenRouter warns prompts routed to MiniMax, including 'zero data retention' traffic, may have been read
items.summary: OpenRouter emailed customers that prompts and outputs sent to MiniMax models may have been accessed by a third party, and removed the Zero Data Retention label from the affected MiniMax endpoints while it investigates. The notice follows a Dragos study by HD Moore that seeded about two million prompts with canary links and credentials; links sent to MiniMax were opened 40 to 130 hours later, including requests flagged ZDR. Per OpenRouter, MiniMax told reseller StreamLake that content moderation was enabled on its endpoints before October 22 and that it has since enabled ZDR. Dragos separately says at least three AI hosting providers were breached by attackers copying customer prompts, none of which knew until notified.
items.why_it_matters: It shows that 'zero data retention' flags on API routers are only as good as every downstream reseller and host, which matters for any enterprise sending code or secrets through aggregators. Expect pressure on routers to audit their supply chains and publish provider-level retention attestations.
key_numbers: ~2/3 of ZDR-flagged requests fetched (Dragos, per reports)

items.title: Bessent says no further China chip curbs needed, H200 stays the threshold, and Huang did not come up with Xi
items.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC on Friday that he does not anticipate any change in US AI-chip policy toward China after the Trump-Xi talks in Shenzhen, saying the two sides had agreed H200s are 'the threshold level of chips' that can be sold to China and that current export controls plus the new remote-access rule are sufficient. He said Jensen Huang was not mentioned in the talks, although Trump told Fox News he 'might have' raised the situation briefly with Xi. Bessent attributed Nvidia's halt of licensed shipments to China to weak demand rather than policy, and reportedly said Commerce had delayed adding Megaspeed to a US restriction list.
items.why_it_matters: It signals no further tightening from Treasury after the Nov 16 remote-access rule, which eases one overhang for Nvidia and AMD. But Bessent's remark that Commerce was slow on Megaspeed adds to the pressure on Lutnick.

learn.title: Build a looped transformer block: reuse weights to buy depth without parameters
learn.why_today: Inkling 2 Mini is described as a looped transformer whose middle layers run several times per token, so its 26.4B parameters understate the compute it spends per token.
learn.explanation: A looped (weight-tied, or universal) transformer applies the same block f_theta R times: x_{r+1} = x_r + f_theta(x_r). Parameter count, and so weight memory, is fixed, while FLOPs and effective depth scale linearly with R, which lets a small model spend more serial computation per token, much like iterating a fixed-point solver. Training backpropagates through all R passes, so gradients for theta are summed over every pass, the same way gradients are shared across time steps in an RNN. That can make optimisation less stable: the residual stream norm grows with each pass, as the toy below shows, which is why pre-norm, careful initialisation or a learned exit or halting rule matter. The trade-off: loops buy depth cheaply in memory but not in latency, because the passes are sequential. The sizes below are illustrative and unrelated to any real model's configuration.
learn.math: x_{r+1} = x_r + f_\theta(x_r),\quad r = 0..R-1, \qquad |\theta| \text{ fixed}, \quad \text{FLOPs} \propto R \cdot 2|\theta| T
learn.python:
# Looped (weight-tied) residual block, stdlib only: one block reused R times.
# Parameters stay fixed while depth and FLOPs grow with R. Illustrative sizes only.
import math, random
random.seed(0)
d, T = 32, 8                                   # width, tokens

def mat(r, c, s): return [[random.gauss(0, s) for _ in range(c)] for _ in range(r)]
def mm(A, B): return [[sum(a * b for a, b in zip(row, col)) for col in zip(*B)] for row in A]
def ln(X): return [[(v - sum(r)/len(r)) / math.sqrt(sum((u - sum(r)/len(r))**2 for u in r)/len(r) + 1e-5) for v in r] for r in X]
def add(A, B): return [[a + b for a, b in zip(ra, rb)] for ra, rb in zip(A, B)]

Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo = (mat(d, d, d**-0.5) for _ in range(4))
W1, W2 = mat(d, 4*d, d**-0.5), mat(4*d, d, (4*d)**-0.5)

def attn(H):
    Q, K, V = mm(H, Wq), mm(H, Wk), mm(H, Wv)
    out = []
    for t in range(T):                          # causal: token t sees 0..t
        s = [sum(q*k for q, k in zip(Q[t], K[j])) / math.sqrt(d) for j in range(t + 1)]
        m = max(s); w = [math.exp(x - m) for x in s]; z = sum(w)
        out.append([sum(w[j]/z * V[j][i] for j in range(t + 1)) for i in range(d)])
    return mm(out, Wo)

def block(X):
    X = add(X, attn(ln(X)))
    return add(X, mm([[max(v, 0) for v in r] for r in mm(ln(X), W1)], W2))

params = 4*d*d + 2*4*d*d
X0 = mat(T, d, 1.0)
for R in (1, 2, 3):
    X = X0
    for _ in range(R):                          # the same weights on every pass
        X = block(X)
    flops = R * T * 2 * params                  # weight matmuls only
    norm = math.sqrt(sum(v*v for r in X for v in r))
    print(f"R={R}: params={params:,}  matmul FLOPs~{flops:,}  |X|={norm:.1f}")

learn.title: Put an interval on a canary hit rate, including the zero-hit case
learn.why_today: OpenRouter's warning followed a Dragos study that seeded about two million prompts with canary links and watched which providers' links were later opened, which is a proportion-estimation problem.
learn.explanation: A canary study turns 'does this provider read prompts?' into counting k hits out of n planted canaries and estimating the rate p. The naive Wald interval p ± z·sqrt(p(1-p)/n) collapses to zero width when k = 0 and goes outside [0, 1] near the edges. The Wilson score interval inverts the score test instead, so it stays inside [0, 1] and keeps close to nominal coverage for small k. With zero hits the useful statement is an upper bound: the 'rule of three' gives p < 3/n at 95%, so clearing a provider at a 0.1% access rate needs about 3,000 clean canaries. Two caveats outweigh the arithmetic: canaries detect only access that triggers them (fetching a link), and hits that cluster in time or by endpoint violate the independence the interval assumes. The counts below are illustrative, not the study's data.
learn.math: \tilde p = \frac{\hat p + \frac{z^2}{2n}}{1+\frac{z^2}{n}}, \quad \text{half-width} = \frac{z\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n} + \frac{z^2}{4n^2}}}{1+\frac{z^2}{n}}, \qquad k=0 \Rightarrow p < 1-0.05^{1/n} \approx 3/n
learn.python:
# Canary study: how sure are you that a provider reads prompts?
# Wilson score interval for a proportion, plus the "zero hits" upper bound.
# Counts below are ILLUSTRATIVE, not the Dragos study's data.
from math import sqrt

def wilson(k, n, z=1.96):
    p = k / n
    c = (p + z*z/(2*n)) / (1 + z*z/n)
    h = z * sqrt(p*(1-p)/n + z*z/(4*n*n)) / (1 + z*z/n)
    return max(0.0, c - h), min(1.0, c + h)

for name, k, n in [("provider A", 0, 5000), ("provider B", 7, 5000), ("provider C", 40, 60)]:
    lo, hi = wilson(k, n)
    print(f"{name}: {k}/{n} canaries fired -> rate in [{lo:.4%}, {hi:.4%}] (95%)")

# Rule of three: with 0 hits in n trials the 95% upper bound is about 3/n.
for n in (100, 1000, 100000):
    print(f"0 hits in {n:>6}: rate < {3/n:.4%}  (exact: {1 - 0.05**(1/n):.4%})")
